# One Histogram Is Enough: Why Knees and Tails Tell the Same Story

*A simple duality between "how big must the threshold be?" and "how many items are above it?" turns an expensive sweep into a single count.*

---

## The question behind the sweep

Imagine you run a service that receives a batch of jobs, and each job has a *demand*: a whole number measuring how much of some resource it needs. It might be tokens in a document, memory for a request, minutes for a repair, or seats for a booking. You must pick a capacity threshold $t$. Any job whose demand is bigger than $t$ overflows: it gets truncated, rejected, or sent somewhere expensive.

You can afford a few overflows, though not many. Call the number of overflows you will tolerate the **gate**, and write it $g$. The natural engineering question is then:

> *What is the smallest threshold that lets through all but at most $g$ jobs?*

That smallest threshold is what we call the **knee** at gate $g$. Plot the knee against the gate and you get a falling staircase. With no tolerance ($g = 0$) the knee is the largest demand. With more tolerance, the knee drops step by step until, once the gate is as large as the whole batch, it reaches zero.

Practitioners often want to compare two collections of demands, say two corpora, two months of traffic, or two languages, by asking whether they have the same knees. The obvious way to answer is a **sweep**: pick several gates, compute the knee of each collection at each gate, and compare. When every cell in a grid of experiments needs its own sweep, the cost adds up quickly.

The results described here show that the sweep is unnecessary. Everything the knees can tell you is already in one object you can compute in a single pass: the **tail histogram**.

---

## Two ways of looking at the same pile

Write the collection of demands as $D$. Repeats are allowed, so $D$ is a *multiset*. There are two natural functions to attach to it.

**The tail.** For a threshold $t$, let
$$\mathrm{tail}_D(t) = \#\{\, d \in D : d > t \,\}$$
be the number of demands that are *strictly larger* than $t$, counted with multiplicity. This is the upper-tail counting function. Statisticians would recognise it as an unnormalised survival function. It can only go down as $t$ grows, and it reaches zero once $t$ is at least the largest demand.

**The knee.** For a gate $g$, let
$$\mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \min\{\, t \ge 0 : \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le g \,\}$$
be the least threshold that at most $g$ demands exceed. Such a threshold always exists, because the largest demand is one.

Take a concrete batch,
$$D = \{7, 5, 5, 3, 1, 0\}.$$
Its tail at thresholds $t = 0, 1, 2, \dots, 7$ is
$$5,\ 4,\ 4,\ 3,\ 3,\ 1,\ 1,\ 0,$$
and its knee at gates $g = 0, 1, 2, \dots, 7$ is
$$7,\ 5,\ 5,\ 3,\ 1,\ 0,\ 0,\ 0.$$

The second list is just the batch sorted from largest to smallest, padded with zeros. That is the first key fact.

---

## The knee is an order statistic

> **Theorem (order statistic).** The knee at gate $g$ is the $g$-th entry, counting from $0$, of the demands listed in decreasing order. When $g$ is at least the number of demands, the knee is $0$.

The reason is simple. Suppose the largest few demands are $7, 5, 5$. A threshold of $5$ is exceeded only by the $7$, so it works at gate $1$. A threshold of $4$ is exceeded by $7, 5, 5$, which is too many. So the knee at gate $1$ is the second-largest demand.

So the "knee" is not a mysterious feature of a curve. It is the demand that sits at rank $g$ from the top. A comparison of knees across several gates is a comparison of order statistics across a range of ranks.

---

## A perfect two-way switch

The deeper structural fact is a two-way switch between the two functions. For every gate $g$ and every threshold $t$:

$$\boxed{\ \mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le t \iff \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le g\ }$$

In words: *the threshold $t$ is at least the knee at gate $g$ exactly when at most $g$ demands exceed $t$.* Mathematicians call this kind of relationship a **Galois connection**. The same pattern links a cumulative distribution function to its quantile function, and the floor function to the inclusion of the integers in the reals.

The switch has a strong consequence. Each function can be recovered from the other. If you know every tail value, you can work out every knee: the knee at $g$ is the first $t$ where the tail falls to $g$ or below. If you know every knee, you know every tail: the tail at $t$ is the number of gates whose knee is still above $t$. Neither function contains any information the other lacks.

---

## The main theorem: knees agree exactly when tails agree

This brings us to the main question. Suppose two collections $D$ and $D'$ have *the same knee at every gate*. What does that say about them?

> **Theorem (knee stability equals tail exchangeability).** For two finite multisets of non-negative integers $D$ and $D'$, the following are equivalent:
>
> 1. $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g)$ for every gate $g$;
> 2. $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) = \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)$ for every threshold $t$;
> 3. $D$ and $D'$ contain exactly the same **positive** demands, with the same multiplicities.

Statements 1 and 2 are equivalent by the two-way switch. To get from 2 to 3, notice that the tail drops by exactly the number of demands equal to $k+1$ as $t$ moves from $k$ to $k+1$:
$$\mathrm{tail}_D(k) = \mathrm{tail}_D(k+1) + \#\{d \in D : d = k+1\}.$$
So the histogram is the *discrete derivative* of the tail. Equal tails give equal histograms at every positive value.

There is one subtlety, and it shows why care pays off. A demand of $0$ never exceeds any threshold $t \ge 0$, so it is invisible to every tail and every knee. The collections $\{4, 2, 2\}$ and $\{0, 2, 4, 0, 2\}$ have identical knees at every gate even though they are different multisets. The tempting slogan "equal knees if and only if equal data" is therefore **false** as stated. The correct version says *equal positive data*. When every demand is positive, which is the usual situation, it really does reduce to plain equality of the multisets.

### You don't even need all the gates

A knee at a gate that is at least as large as the whole collection is automatically $0$. So a finite check is enough:

> **Theorem (finite sweep).** $D$ and $D'$ have equal knees at every gate as soon as they have equal knees at the gates $g = 0, 1, \dots, \max(|D|, |D'|) - 1$.

---

## Windows of gates and bands of counts

In practice nobody cares about every gate. You might care about gates $10$ through $19$, the regime where "a handful of overflows is fine". Can the histogram still decide the question when you only want the knees to agree on a **window** of gates?

The answer is yes, and the formula is a pleasant surprise. Define the clamp of a count $x$ to the band $[a, a+w]$:
$$\mathrm{clamp}_{[a,a+w]}(x) = \min\big(\max(x, a),\ a+w\big).$$
Values below $a$ are pushed up to $a$, values above $a+w$ are pushed down to $a+w$, and values inside the band are left alone.

> **Theorem (window).** Two collections have equal knees at every gate $g$ with $a \le g < a + w$ if and only if, at every threshold $t$,
> $$\mathrm{clamp}_{[a,a+w]}\big(\mathrm{tail}_D(t)\big) = \mathrm{clamp}_{[a,a+w]}\big(\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)\big).$$

Equivalently, when the window is non-empty, at each threshold the two tails must:

* agree on whether they are **at or below** $a$,
* agree on whether they are **at or above** $a + w$, and
* be exactly **equal** whenever they lie strictly between $a$ and $a + w$.

So a window of $w$ gates corresponds to a band of counts one unit wider, $[a, a+w]$. Inside the band the tails must match exactly. Outside it, only the side matters.

For example, take $D = \{9, 6, 4, 2\}$ and $D' = \{8, 6, 4, 1, 1\}$. Their knee profiles are $9, 6, 4, 2, 0$ and $8, 6, 4, 1, 1$. They disagree at gates $0$, $3$ and $4$ but agree on the window of gates $1$ and $2$. Clamping both tails to the band $[1, 3]$ gives the same sequence $3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1$ for both collections, as the theorem predicts.

### Beware the obvious guess

The "obvious" version of the window statement is wrong. It says that the knees agree on gates $a$ through $b$ exactly when the tails agree whenever the count lies in $[a, b]$. Take $D = \{3\}$, $D' = \{2\}$, and the single gate $1$. Both knees are $0$, because one overflow is allowed and there is only one demand. Yet at threshold $t = 2$ the tail of $D$ is $1$, which lies in $[1,1]$, while the tail of $D'$ is $0$. The naive band condition fails even though the knees agree.

The fix is the clamp. Counts at the *edge* of the band only need to land on the same side, not to be equal. This is the kind of off-by-one trap that is easy to miss in an informal argument and that a careful statement rules out.

---

## Stability: what happens when data is noisy?

Real collections are never exactly equal, so the most useful results are quantitative. The same two-way switch gives a precise, loss-free conversion between "tails are close" and "knees are close".

> **Theorem (gate shift).** For any shift $k \ge 0$, the following are equivalent:
>
> * for every gate $g$, $\ \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g + k) \le \mathrm{knee}_D(g)$;
> * for every threshold $t$, $\ \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t) \le \mathrm{tail}_D(t) + k$.

So if the two tails never differ by more than $k$ in either direction, each knee profile is sandwiched by the other, shifted by $k$ gates:
$$\mathrm{knee}_{D}(g + k) \le \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g) \quad\text{and}\quad \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g + k) \le \mathrm{knee}_{D}(g).$$

Two practical corollaries follow.

* **Contamination.** If you add a collection $E$ of extra demands, knees can only go up, and by no more than $|E|$ gates:
  $$\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le \mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g), \qquad \mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g + |E|) \le \mathrm{knee}_D(g).$$
* **Pooling.** When two collections are merged, tails simply add: $\mathrm{tail}_{D+E} = \mathrm{tail}_D + \mathrm{tail}_E$. On the knee side this gives
  $$\max\big(\mathrm{knee}_D(g), \mathrm{knee}_E(g)\big) \le \mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g), \qquad \mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g+h) \le \max\big(\mathrm{knee}_D(g), \mathrm{knee}_E(h)\big).$$

---

## A picture from the 19th century

All of this has a classical picture behind it. Draw the demands as rows of boxes, longest row first. This is the **Ferrers diagram** familiar from the theory of integer partitions. For $D = \{5, 3, 3, 1\}$:

```
#####     knee at gate 0 = 5
###       knee at gate 1 = 3
###       knee at gate 2 = 3
#         knee at gate 3 = 1
```

The **rows** have lengths equal to the knees. The **columns** have heights $4, 3, 3, 1, 1$, and these are exactly the tail values at $t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$. Knees and tails are *conjugate partitions*: the same diagram read across or down. Two identities follow at once:
$$\mathrm{tail}_D(t) = \#\{\, g < |D| : \mathrm{knee}_D(g) > t \,\}, \qquad \mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \#\{\, t < \max D : \mathrm{tail}_D(t) > g \,\}.$$
Counting the boxes both ways gives the **area identity**:
$$\sum_{g=0}^{|D|-1} \mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \sum_{d \in D} d.$$
The knees always add up to the total demand.

---

## Why this matters

The practical message is that **a single tail histogram per collection is a sufficient statistic for every knee question**:

* Do two collections have identical knees? Compare their positive histograms.
* Do they agree on a window of gates? Clamp their tails to the matching band and compare.
* How far apart can their knees be? Take the largest gap between their tails. That gap bounds the gate shift, with no loss.

A histogram costs one pass over the data. It can be built in pieces and added up, since tails of pooled collections simply add. It can be stored compactly and reused for any gate window chosen later. Work that used to need a full sweep of knee computations for every cell of an experimental grid now needs one count per collection. This makes larger collections, and collections with fewer documents, affordable to analyse.

The idea underneath is old and simple. A threshold and a count of exceedances are two sides of one Galois connection, and an order statistic is the inverse of a counting function. Seeing the knee this way turns a property that seemed to need many measurements into one that a single count already settles.

---

## Where next?

Several natural extensions remain open:

* **A metric.** The gate-shift theorem already implies that the smallest gate shift making each knee profile dominate the other equals the largest gap between the tails. Developing this number into a full Kolmogorov-type distance between collections, with its triangle inequality and normalised versions, would give one figure per pair of collections that bounds every knee discrepancy.
* **Weights.** When demands carry real-valued weights, the same switch should hold for weighted tails, which matters when items count by size rather than by number.
* **Sampling.** If a subsample's tail is uniformly close to the scaled population tail, the gate-shift theorem converts that into a knee guarantee with no extra loss.
* **Pooling.** Since tails add under merging, knee profiles of a large collection could be assembled from histograms of its shards.

Each of these follows the pattern of this article. Translate the question about knees into a question about tails, answer it there where the arithmetic is easy, and translate back.

# Knee Stability Is Equivalent to Tail-Exchangeability

### Order statistics, Galois connections, and count bands for finite demand multisets

**Author:** Aristotle

**Date:** 2026-10-26

---

## Abstract

A *demand multiset* is a finite multiset $D$ of non-negative integers. Its *upper-tail counting function* $\mathrm{tail}_D(t)$ counts the demands strictly larger than a threshold $t$. Its *knee* at gate $g$, $\mathrm{knee}_D(g)$, is the least threshold exceeded by at most $g$ demands. We prove that knees and tails form a Galois connection, $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le t \iff \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le g$, and that the knee at gate $g$ is the $g$-th largest demand (indexed from $0$, and $0$ past the end).

From this we derive a complete answer to the question of when two demand multisets "look the same through their knees". Equal knees at every gate is equivalent to equal tail functions, and also to equality of the sub-multisets of *positive* demands. The unguarded statement with equality of full multisets is false. Equal knees on a gate window $a \le g < a + w$ is equivalent to equality of the tail functions after clamping to the count band $[a, a+w]$. We show that the naive closed-band formulation fails. A sweep over $\max(|D|, |D'|)$ gates decides all-gate equality.

We also prove the conjugate-partition duality between knees and tails, the area identity $\sum_{g<|D|} \mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \sum D$, and a sharp quantitative stability theorem. A $k$-gate shift between knee profiles is equivalent to a uniform additive bound $k$ between tails. This gives contamination and merge bounds. The practical consequence is that a single tail histogram per collection is a sufficient statistic for every question about knees, so multi-gate sweeps can be replaced by one counting pass.

---

## 1. Introduction

Many empirical procedures summarise a collection of non-negative integer "demands" by a threshold that tolerates a prescribed number of exceedances. The demands might be document lengths, request sizes, latencies or resource requirements. Given a *gate* $g$, meaning the number of exceedances one is willing to tolerate, the *knee* is the smallest threshold exceeded by at most $g$ items. Comparing two collections by their knees at a handful of gates is common. We call this *knee stability*. It is usually done by recomputing knees at each gate for each collection, a *sweep*.

This paper studies knee stability exactly. The central observation is elementary but has strong consequences:

> *The knee is an order statistic, so agreement of knees on an interval of gates is exactly agreement of the inverse distribution function on the corresponding interval of ranks.*

We make this precise through a Galois connection between the knee function and the upper-tail counting function. We then answer three questions completely.

1. **All gates.** When do two collections have the same knee at *every* gate? (Theorem 4.3.)
2. **Gate windows.** When do they have the same knee on a *window* of gates? (Theorem 5.2 and Theorem 5.3.) We also show that a natural but wrong formulation fails (Proposition 5.4).
3. **Approximate agreement.** How does closeness of the data control closeness of knees? (Theorem 7.1 and its corollaries.)

In every case the answer can be read off a single object, the tail histogram, with no sweep. Section 6 adds the combinatorial picture: knees and tails are conjugate partitions, and their common area is the total demand.

### 1.1 Notation and conventions

All numbers are natural numbers $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$. A *multiset* $D$ over $\mathbb{N}$ is a finite unordered collection with repetitions. We write $|D|$ for its cardinality counted with multiplicity, $\#_D(v)$ for the multiplicity of $v$ in $D$, $\max D$ for its largest element (with $\max \varnothing = 0$), and $\sum D$ for the sum of its elements. $D + E$ is the multiset union, which adds multiplicities. For a predicate $P$, $D|_P$ is the sub-multiset of elements satisfying $P$. In particular $D|_{>0}$ is the multiset of positive demands of $D$.

---

## 2. Definitions

**Definition 2.1 (Upper-tail counting function).** For a demand multiset $D$ and a threshold $t \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$\mathrm{tail}_D(t) \;=\; \big|\, D|_{> t} \,\big| \;=\; \#\{\, d \in D : d > t \,\}\quad(\text{with multiplicity}).$$

**Definition 2.2 (Knee).** For a gate $g \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \;=\; \min\{\, t \in \mathbb{N} : \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le g \,\}.$$
The set is non-empty because $\mathrm{tail}_D(\max D) = 0 \le g$ (Lemma 3.1), so the minimum exists.

**Definition 2.3 (Clamp).** For $a, w, x \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$\mathrm{clamp}_{a,w}(x) \;=\; \min\big(\max(x, a),\, a + w\big),$$
the projection of $x$ onto the integer interval $[a, a+w]$.

**Definition 2.4 (Decreasing arrangement).** $\mathrm{sort}^{\downarrow}(D) = (d_0 \ge d_1 \ge \dots \ge d_{n-1})$ is the list of elements of $D$ in non-increasing order, with $n = |D|$. For $g \ge n$ we set $d_g := 0$.

**Running example.** For $D = \{7, 5, 5, 3, 1, 0\}$:

| $t$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{tail}_D(t)$ | 5 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

| $g$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{knee}_D(g)$ | 7 | 5 | 5 | 3 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

---

## 3. Elementary properties and the Galois connection

**Lemma 3.1 (Basic properties of the tail).**
1. If every $d \in D$ satisfies $d \le t$, then $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) = 0$. In particular $\mathrm{tail}_D(\max D) = 0$.
2. $\mathrm{tail}_D$ is antitone: $s \le t \Rightarrow \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le \mathrm{tail}_D(s)$.
3. $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le |D|$.
4. $\mathrm{tail}_{D+E}(t) = \mathrm{tail}_D(t) + \mathrm{tail}_E(t)$, and $\mathrm{tail}_{\{a\} + D}(t) = \mathrm{tail}_D(t) + [t < a]$.

*Proof sketch.* (1) The filter $D|_{>t}$ is empty. (2) $s \le t$ gives $D|_{>t} \subseteq D|_{>s}$. (3) A sub-multiset is no larger than the whole. (4) Filtering commutes with multiset union, and cardinality is additive. $\square$

**Theorem 3.2 (Galois connection).** For all $D$, $g$, $t$:
$$\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le t \iff \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le g.$$

*Proof.* By definition of the minimum, $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le t$ holds iff there is some $m \le t$ with $\mathrm{tail}_D(m) \le g$. If such an $m$ exists, antitonicity gives $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le \mathrm{tail}_D(m) \le g$. Conversely take $m = t$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.3.** For all $D$, $g$, $t$:
1. $t < \mathrm{knee}_D(g) \iff g < \mathrm{tail}_D(t)$;
2. $\mathrm{tail}_D(\mathrm{knee}_D(g)) \le g$;
3. $\mathrm{knee}_D$ is antitone in $g$;
4. $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le \max D$;
5. $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) = 0 \iff \mathrm{tail}_D(0) \le g$, that is, iff $D$ has at most $g$ positive demands.

*Proof sketch.* (1) is the contrapositive of Theorem 3.2. (2) takes $t = \mathrm{knee}_D(g)$. For (3), if $g \le h$ then $\mathrm{tail}_D(\mathrm{knee}_D(g)) \le g \le h$, so $\mathrm{knee}_D(h) \le \mathrm{knee}_D(g)$. (4) uses Lemma 3.1(1). (5) takes $t = 0$. $\square$

**Lemma 3.4 (Pointwise criterion).** For a fixed gate $g$,
$$\mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g) \iff \forall t,\; \big(\mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le g \iff \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t) \le g\big).$$

*Proof sketch.* By Theorem 3.2 the right-hand side says that the up-sets $\{t : \mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le t\}$ and $\{t : \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g) \le t\}$ coincide. Two natural numbers with the same up-set are equal. $\square$

This lemma is the engine behind all later results. A knee at a single gate depends on the tail only through the binary classification "$\le g$" versus "$> g$".

### 3.1 The knee is an order statistic

**Theorem 3.5 (Order statistic).** For every $D$ and every $g$,
$$\mathrm{knee}_D(g) = d_g,$$
the $g$-th entry (0-indexed) of $\mathrm{sort}^{\downarrow}(D)$, and $0$ when $g \ge |D|$.

*Proof sketch.* First, $\mathrm{tail}_D(t)$ equals the number of entries of the list $\mathrm{sort}^{\downarrow}(D)$ exceeding $t$, since the list is a permutation of $D$. Next we prove, by induction on a non-increasing list $L = (x, L')$, that
$$L_g \le t \iff \#\{\text{entries of } L \text{ exceeding } t\} \le g$$
(with $L_g := 0$ past the end).

* For $g = 0$: if $x \le t$, every entry of $L'$ is $\le x \le t$, so the count is $0$. If $x > t$, the count is at least $1$.
* For $g = g' + 1$: if $x > t$ the count is $1$ plus the count for $L'$, and the induction hypothesis applies to $L'_{g'}$. If $x \le t$ both sides are true, since $L'_{g'} \le x \le t$ (or $L'_{g'} = 0$).

Hence $d_g$ satisfies the same Galois characterisation as $\mathrm{knee}_D(g)$. Two quantities with identical up-sets are equal. $\square$

For instance, the knee profile $7,5,5,3,1,0,0,\dots$ in the running example is exactly $\mathrm{sort}^{\downarrow}(D)$ padded with zeros.

---

## 4. Agreement at all gates

**Theorem 4.1 (Knee stability ⟺ tail exchangeability).** For all demand multisets $D, D'$,
$$\big(\forall g,\ \mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g)\big) \iff \big(\forall t,\ \mathrm{tail}_D(t) = \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)\big).$$

*Proof.* ($\Leftarrow$) Apply Lemma 3.4 at each gate. ($\Rightarrow$) Fix $t$. By Theorem 3.2 with $g = \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)$, $\mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g) \le t$. Hence $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le t$, and so $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)$. The reverse inequality follows by symmetry. $\square$

To pass from tails to the data itself we need the discrete derivative of the tail.

**Lemma 4.2 (Histogram as discrete derivative).** For all $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$\mathrm{tail}_D(k) = \mathrm{tail}_D(k+1) + \#_D(k+1).$$
Moreover $\mathrm{tail}_{D|_{>0}}(t) = \mathrm{tail}_D(t)$ for all $t$.

*Proof sketch.* Induct on $D$ using Lemma 3.1(4). Adding an element $a$ changes both sides by $[k < a] = [k+1 < a] + [a = k+1]$. For the second claim, $d > t \ge 0$ already implies $d > 0$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.3 (Main theorem, all gates).** For all demand multisets $D, D'$, the following are equivalent:
1. $\mathrm{knee}_D = \mathrm{knee}_{D'}$ (equal knees at every gate);
2. $\mathrm{tail}_D = \mathrm{tail}_{D'}$ (equal upper-tail counting functions);
3. $D|_{>0} = D'|_{>0}$ (equal multisets of positive demands).

*Proof sketch.* (1)⟺(2) is Theorem 4.1. (2)⟹(3): for each $v = k + 1 \ge 1$, Lemma 4.2 gives $\#_D(k+1) = \mathrm{tail}_D(k) - \mathrm{tail}_D(k+1)$, and the same for $D'$. Multiplicities at $0$ are removed by the filter on both sides. (3)⟹(2): $\mathrm{tail}_D = \mathrm{tail}_{D|_{>0}} = \mathrm{tail}_{D'|_{>0}} = \mathrm{tail}_{D'}$ by the second part of Lemma 4.2. $\square$

**Corollary 4.4 (Positive demands).** If every element of $D$ and of $D'$ is positive, then $\mathrm{knee}_D = \mathrm{knee}_{D'} \iff D = D'$.

**Proposition 4.5 (The unguarded statement is false).** It is not true that $\mathrm{knee}_D = \mathrm{knee}_{D'}$ implies $D = D'$ for all $D, D'$.

*Proof.* Take $D = \{0\}$ and $D' = \varnothing$. Both have no positive demands, so their knees agree by Theorem 4.3, yet $D \ne D'$. A less trivial instance is $\{4,2,2\}$ versus $\{0,2,4,0,2\}$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.6 (Finite sweep).** Let $m = \max(|D|, |D'|)$. Then
$$\mathrm{knee}_D = \mathrm{knee}_{D'} \iff \forall g < m,\ \mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g).$$

*Proof sketch.* For $g \ge m$ we have $\mathrm{tail}_D(0) \le |D| \le g$, so $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) = 0$ by Corollary 3.3(5). Likewise $\mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g) = 0$. $\square$

---

## 5. Agreement on a window of gates

We now localise Theorem 4.1 to a *gate window* $W = \{g : a \le g < a + w\}$ of width $w$.

**Lemma 5.1.** For fixed $t$ and $x = \mathrm{tail}_D(t)$, $y = \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)$:
$$\big(\forall g \in W,\ x \le g \iff y \le g\big) \iff \mathrm{clamp}_{a,w}(x) = \mathrm{clamp}_{a,w}(y).$$

*Proof sketch.* Suppose $\mathrm{clamp}(x) < \mathrm{clamp}(y)$. Then $g := \mathrm{clamp}(x)$ lies in $W$, because $a \le g$ and $g < \mathrm{clamp}(y) \le a + w$. We also have $x \le g$ and $y > g$, which contradicts the left-hand side. The other order is symmetric. Conversely, if the clamps agree then for each $g \in W$ the comparison $x \le g$ is decided by $\mathrm{clamp}(x)$, since $a \le g < a + w$. So it agrees with $y \le g$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.2 (Main theorem, gate window).** For all $D, D'$ and $a, w \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$\big(\forall g,\ a \le g < a + w \Rightarrow \mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g)\big) \iff \big(\forall t,\ \mathrm{clamp}_{a,w}(\mathrm{tail}_D(t)) = \mathrm{clamp}_{a,w}(\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t))\big).$$

*Proof.* Apply Lemma 3.4 at each $g \in W$. Exchange the quantifiers over $g$ and $t$, then apply Lemma 5.1 at each $t$. $\square$

In the language of distribution functions, the knee at gate $g$ is the rank-$g$ value of the generalised inverse of $\mathrm{tail}_D$. Agreement of the inverse on the rank interval $[a, a+w)$ is agreement of the function itself after projection onto the *count band* $[a, a+w]$. This band is one unit wider than the gate window.

**Theorem 5.3 (Band formulation).** Assume $w > 0$. The window condition of Theorem 5.2 is equivalent to the following: for every threshold $t$,
1. $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le a \iff \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t) \le a$ (same "at or below band" classification);
2. $a + w \le \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \iff a + w \le \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)$ (same "at or above band" classification);
3. if $a < \mathrm{tail}_D(t) < a + w$ then $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) = \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)$ (exact agreement in the open band).

*Proof sketch.* Fix $t$ and put $x = \mathrm{tail}_D(t)$, $y = \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)$. With $w > 0$ the three cases $x \le a$, $a < x < a + w$, $x \ge a + w$ give $\mathrm{clamp}(x) = a$, $\mathrm{clamp}(x) = x$ and $\mathrm{clamp}(x) = a + w$ respectively. These values are pairwise distinct when $w > 0$, so equality of clamps is exactly conditions 1–3. Each direction is a short case analysis in linear arithmetic. $\square$

**Example 5.4.** Let $D = \{9, 6, 4, 2\}$ and $D' = \{8, 6, 4, 1, 1\}$, with knee profiles $(9,6,4,2,0,\dots)$ and $(8,6,4,1,1,0,\dots)$. They agree exactly on the window $\{1, 2\}$, so $a = 1$ and $w = 2$. Their tails at $t = 0, \dots, 9$ are
$$\mathrm{tail}_D = (4,4,3,3,2,2,1,1,1,0), \qquad \mathrm{tail}_{D'} = (5,3,3,3,2,2,1,1,0,0).$$
They differ at $t = 0$, $1$ and $8$, but clamping to $[1, 3]$ gives $(3,3,3,3,2,2,1,1,1,1)$ for both.

**Proposition 5.5 (The naive closed-band formulation is false).** The following statement fails in general: for all $D, D'$ and all $a, b$,
$$\big(\forall g \in [a,b],\ \mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g)\big) \iff \big(\forall t,\ a \le \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le b \Rightarrow \mathrm{tail}_D(t) = \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)\big).$$

*Proof.* Take $D = \{3\}$, $D' = \{2\}$ and $a = b = 1$. Both knees at gate $1$ equal $0$, since each multiset has only one positive demand (Corollary 3.3(5)). So the left side holds. At $t = 2$, however, $\mathrm{tail}_D(2) = 1 \in [1,1]$ while $\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(2) = 0$. So the right side fails. $\square$

The counterexample shows where the clamp is needed. On the *boundary* of the band, here the value $a = 1$, the tails need only fall on the same side, not coincide.

---

## 6. Conjugate-partition duality and the area identity

Draw $D$ as a Ferrers diagram whose rows, longest first, have lengths $d_0 \ge d_1 \ge \dots$. By Theorem 3.5 the row lengths are the knees. The column heights are the tails.

**Theorem 6.1 (Conjugate duality).** For all $D$, $t$, $g$:
$$\mathrm{tail}_D(t) = \#\{\, g < |D| : t < \mathrm{knee}_D(g) \,\}, \qquad \mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \#\{\, t < \max D : g < \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \,\}.$$

*Proof sketch.* By Corollary 3.3(1), $t < \mathrm{knee}_D(g) \iff g < \mathrm{tail}_D(t)$. So the first set is $\{g < |D| : g < \mathrm{tail}_D(t)\} = \{0, \dots, \mathrm{tail}_D(t) - 1\}$, using $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le |D|$. Likewise the second set is $\{0, \dots, \mathrm{knee}_D(g) - 1\}$, using $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le \max D$. $\square$

Thus $\mathrm{tail}_D$ and $\mathrm{knee}_D$, viewed as partitions, are conjugate to each other.

**Theorem 6.2 (Area identity).**
$$\sum_{g=0}^{|D|-1} \mathrm{knee}_D(g) \;=\; \sum_{d \in D} d.$$

*Proof sketch.* By Theorem 3.5 the left side is $\sum_{g < |D|} d_g$, the sum of the list $\mathrm{sort}^{\downarrow}(D)$, which is $\sum D$. (Counting boxes by columns gives the dual identity $\sum_{t < \max D} \mathrm{tail}_D(t) = \sum D$.) $\square$

In the running example, $7 + 5 + 5 + 3 + 1 + 0 = 21 = 5 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 1 + 1$.

---

## 7. Quantitative stability

Exact equality is rarely available in practice. The Galois connection also transfers *inequalities* between the two sides with no loss.

**Theorem 7.1 (Gate-shift ⟺ uniform tail bound).** For all $D, D'$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$:
$$\big(\forall g,\ \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g + k) \le \mathrm{knee}_D(g)\big) \iff \big(\forall t,\ \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t) \le \mathrm{tail}_D(t) + k\big).$$

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) Fix $t$ and set $g = \mathrm{tail}_D(t)$. By Theorem 3.2, $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le t$, so $\mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g + k) \le t$. By Theorem 3.2 again, $\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t) \le g + k$. ($\Leftarrow$) Fix $g$. By Theorem 3.2 it suffices to show $\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(\mathrm{knee}_D(g)) \le g + k$. The hypothesis gives $\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(\mathrm{knee}_D(g)) \le \mathrm{tail}_D(\mathrm{knee}_D(g)) + k$, and Corollary 3.3(2) gives $\mathrm{tail}_D(\mathrm{knee}_D(g)) \le g$. $\square$

**Corollary 7.2 (Lipschitz sandwich).** If $|\mathrm{tail}_D(t) - \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)| \le k$ for all $t$, then for every gate $g$,
$$\mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g + k) \le \mathrm{knee}_D(g) \quad\text{and}\quad \mathrm{knee}_D(g + k) \le \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g).$$

**Corollary 7.3 (Contamination).** For all $D, E$ and $g$,
$$\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le \mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g) \quad\text{and}\quad \mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g + |E|) \le \mathrm{knee}_D(g).$$

*Proof sketch.* By Lemma 3.1(4) and (3), $\mathrm{tail}_D \le \mathrm{tail}_{D+E} = \mathrm{tail}_D + \mathrm{tail}_E \le \mathrm{tail}_D + |E|$. Apply Theorem 7.1 with $k = 0$ (with the roles of $D$ and $D+E$ swapped) and with $k = |E|$. $\square$

**Corollary 7.4 (Merge bounds).** For all $D, E$ and gates $g, h$:
$$\max\big(\mathrm{knee}_D(g), \mathrm{knee}_E(g)\big) \le \mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g), \qquad \mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g + h) \le \max\big(\mathrm{knee}_D(g), \mathrm{knee}_E(h)\big).$$

*Proof sketch.* The first inequality is Corollary 7.3 applied to $D$ and to $E$. For the second, put $m = \max(\mathrm{knee}_D(g), \mathrm{knee}_E(h))$. By antitonicity and Corollary 3.3(2), $\mathrm{tail}_{D+E}(m) = \mathrm{tail}_D(m) + \mathrm{tail}_E(m) \le g + h$. Then apply Theorem 3.2. $\square$

---

## 8. Algorithms

The results above make the tail histogram a sufficient statistic for every knee question. We record the resulting procedures. Throughout, $n = |D|$ and $V$ is the number of distinct values.

**Algorithm A (tail histogram).** One pass builds the histogram $h(v) = \#_D(v)$. Sorting the distinct values in decreasing order and accumulating suffix sums gives the step function $\mathrm{tail}_D$, stored as $V$ breakpoints. Cost: $O(n + V \log V)$ time and $O(V)$ space. Histograms of shards combine by addition (Lemma 3.1(4)).

**Algorithm B (knee from histogram).** By Theorem 3.2, $\mathrm{knee}_D(g)$ is the least breakpoint $t$ with $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le g$. Binary search over the breakpoints costs $O(\log V)$ per gate. Equivalently, by Theorem 3.5, it is the $g$-th largest element.

**Algorithm C (all-gate equality test).** By Theorem 4.3, compare the histograms restricted to positive values. Cost $O(V + V')$ after Algorithm A. No gate sweep is needed. If one insists on comparing knees directly, Theorem 4.6 bounds the sweep at $\max(|D|, |D'|)$ gates.

**Algorithm D (window equality test).** By Theorem 5.2, merge the breakpoint sets of $\mathrm{tail}_D$ and $\mathrm{tail}_{D'}$. Between consecutive breakpoints both tails are constant. Compare $\mathrm{clamp}_{a,w}$ of the two values on each piece. Cost $O(V + V')$ for any window, so one histogram per collection serves all windows chosen later.

**Algorithm E (gate-shift distance).** Compute $k^\ast = \max_t |\mathrm{tail}_D(t) - \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)|$ over the merged breakpoints, in $O(V + V')$. By Corollary 7.2, each knee profile dominates the other after a shift of $k^\ast$ gates. By the forward direction of Theorem 7.1, no smaller *mutual* shift is possible. So $k^\ast$ is the exact minimal mutual gate shift.

---

## 9. Applications and discussion

**From sweeps to histograms.** A typical comparison computes knees of two collections at a grid of gates and declares the collections "knee-stable" if the knees match. Theorems 4.3 and 5.2 show that the outcome of any such sweep, at all gates or on any window, is determined by the tail histograms alone. A sweep over $G$ gates for each of $C$ cells costs $G \cdot C$ knee computations, and each one requires a pass or a sort. The histogram approach costs one pass per collection and $O(V)$ per comparison afterwards. This matters most when collections are large, or when collections are numerous but small, as with many low-resource sub-domains.

**Robustness.** Theorem 7.1 is sharp: it is an equivalence, not merely an implication. So the supremum gap between tails is *the* right measure of knee discrepancy. Corollary 7.3 says that injecting $|E|$ spurious items can move knees by at most $|E|$ gates, and only upward. This gives a deterministic certificate for contaminated or partially deduplicated data.

**Zero demands.** Proposition 4.5 is a reminder that knees are blind to zero demands. Any claim that knee stability identifies a collection must be stated for the positive part. Such a claim is exact only when all demands are positive (Corollary 4.4).

**Boundary effects.** Proposition 5.5 shows that the gate window and the count band are offset by one, $[a, a+w)$ versus $[a, a+w]$, and that the boundary of the band carries only one bit of information per threshold (which side). Informal arguments that miss this offset give statements that are false.

**Relation to classical notions.** Theorem 3.2 is the discrete form of the duality between a survival function and its quantile function. Theorem 6.1 is the classical conjugation of integer partitions, and Theorem 6.2 is the statement that a partition and its conjugate have the same size. The contribution here is the exact window theorem, with its band offset and boundary behaviour, and the sharp shift–bound equivalence, both stated in a form that applies directly to comparing empirical collections.

---

## 10. Future work

1. **Gate-shift metric as a Kolmogorov distance.** Algorithm E shows, as a direct consequence of Theorem 7.1, that the least $k$ such that each knee profile dominates the other after a shift of $k$ gates equals $\sup_t |\mathrm{tail}_D(t) - \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)|$. The next step is to develop this quantity as a metric in its own right: the $\ell^\infty$ distance between conjugate partitions, that is, an unnormalised Lévy–Kolmogorov distance on demand distributions, with its triangle inequality, its behaviour under normalisation by $|D|$, and its interaction with pooling.
2. **Weighted and fractional gates.** For demands with real weights, the knee at a real gate $\gamma$ should be the generalised inverse of the weighted tail, and window agreement should be equivalent to agreement of clamped weighted tails. Only the Galois connection was used above, and it holds for any right-continuous antitone tail.
3. **Sampling stability.** If a subsample of size $n$ has empirical tail within $\varepsilon n$ of the scaled population tail (a Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz-type event), every sampled knee should lie between the population knees at gates $g \pm \varepsilon n$. The deterministic sandwich of Corollary 7.2 converts any uniform tail bound into a knee bound with no extra loss.
4. **Pooling via conjugate addition.** Tails add under pooling. So the knee profile of $D + E$ is the conjugate of the sum of the conjugates (the union of the partitions), and all-gate agreement is preserved when pooling with a common collection $E$. Window agreement, however, is *not* preserved in general. The empty multiset and $\{1\}$ have equal knees ($0$) at gate $1$, but after pooling each with $E = \{1\}$ the knees at gate $1$ are $0$ and $1$. The open problem is to find how the window must move or shrink under pooling. A complete answer would let knee profiles on chosen windows be assembled from histograms of shards.

---

## 11. Conclusion

The knee of a demand multiset at a gate is an order statistic, and it is linked to the upper-tail counting function by a Galois connection. All the results here follow from that one fact. Equal knees at all gates is the same as equal tails, which is the same as equal positive data. Equal knees on a gate window is the same as equal tails clamped to a count band one unit wider. Closeness of tails in sup norm is the same as closeness of knees up to a gate shift. Each statement is an exact equivalence, and each comes with a counterexample showing where a looser version fails. As a result, any question about knees can be answered from a single tail histogram per collection, with no sweep.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Knee stability is equivalent to tail-exchangeability -- numerical companion.

A *demand multiset* D is a finite list of non-negative integers (order irrelevant).

  tail(D, t)  = #{ d in D : d > t }                 (upper-tail counting function)
  knee(D, g)  = least t >= 0 with tail(D, t) <= g    (knee at gate g)

This script checks, on hand-picked and random examples, every result of the paper:

  1. Galois connection      knee(D,g) <= t  <=>  tail(D,t) <= g
  2. Order statistic        knee(D,g) = g-th largest demand (0-indexed), 0 past the end
  3. All-gate theorem       knee(D,.) = knee(D',.) <=> tail(D,.) = tail(D',.)
                            <=> D and D' have the same positive demands
  4. Window theorem         knees agree for a <= g < a+w
                            <=> clamp_[a,a+w] tail(D,t) = clamp_[a,a+w] tail(D',t) for all t
  5. Naive closed band is false (explicit counterexample)
  6. Finite sweep           all-gate equality is decided by gates g < max(|D|,|D'|)
  7. Conjugate duality and the area identity  sum_{g<|D|} knee(D,g) = sum(D)
  8. Stability              (forall g: knee(D',g+k) <= knee(D,g)) <=> (forall t: tail(D',t) <= tail(D,t)+k)
                            contamination and merge bounds

Only the Python standard library is used.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import random
from collections import Counter
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Demands = Sequence[int]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core definitions
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def tail(D: Demands, t: int) -> int:
    """Number of demands strictly greater than the threshold t."""
    return sum(1 for d in D if d > t)


def knee(D: Demands, g: int) -> int:
    """Least threshold t >= 0 exceeded by at most g demands (definition by search)."""
    t = 0
    while tail(D, t) > g:
        t += 1
    return t


def knee_order_statistic(D: Demands, g: int) -> int:
    """The g-th entry (0-indexed) of D sorted in decreasing order; 0 past the end."""
    s = sorted(D, reverse=True)
    return s[g] if g < len(s) else 0


def tail_profile(D: Demands) -> List[int]:
    """tail(D, t) for t = 0 .. max(D) (it is 0 from max(D) on)."""
    top = max(D, default=0)
    return [tail(D, t) for t in range(top + 1)]


def knee_profile(D: Demands, gates: int | None = None) -> List[int]:
    """knee(D, g) for g = 0 .. gates-1 (default |D|)."""
    n = len(D) if gates is None else gates
    return [knee(D, g) for g in range(n)]


def tail_from_histogram(hist: Dict[int, int], t: int) -> int:
    """Tail computed from a histogram {value: multiplicity} -- 'one histogram per corpus'."""
    return sum(c for v, c in hist.items() if v > t)


def clamp_band(a: int, w: int, x: int) -> int:
    """Clamp the count x to the band [a, a+w]."""
    return min(max(x, a), a + w)


def positive_part(D: Demands) -> Counter:
    return Counter(d for d in D if d > 0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Predicates corresponding to the theorems
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def knees_agree_on_window(D: Demands, E: Demands, a: int, w: int) -> bool:
    return all(knee(D, g) == knee(E, g) for g in range(a, a + w))


def clamped_tails_agree(D: Demands, E: Demands, a: int, w: int) -> bool:
    top = max(max(D, default=0), max(E, default=0))
    return all(clamp_band(a, w, tail(D, t)) == clamp_band(a, w, tail(E, t))
               for t in range(top + 1))


def band_form_agrees(D: Demands, E: Demands, a: int, w: int) -> bool:
    """Below-band / above-band classification agrees and tails coincide in the open band."""
    top = max(max(D, default=0), max(E, default=0))
    for t in range(top + 1):
        x, y = tail(D, t), tail(E, t)
        if (x <= a) != (y <= a):
            return False
        if (x >= a + w) != (y >= a + w):
            return False
        if a < x < a + w and x != y:
            return False
    return True


def all_knees_agree(D: Demands, E: Demands) -> bool:
    gates = max(len(D), len(E)) + 3  # a few extra gates beyond the sweep bound
    return all(knee(D, g) == knee(E, g) for g in range(gates))


def all_tails_agree(D: Demands, E: Demands) -> bool:
    top = max(max(D, default=0), max(E, default=0)) + 2
    return all(tail(D, t) == tail(E, t) for t in range(top))


def random_demands(rng: random.Random, n_max: int = 7, v_max: int = 6) -> List[int]:
    return [rng.randint(0, v_max) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, n_max))]


def check(name: str, ok: bool) -> None:
    print(f"  [{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name}")
    if not ok:
        raise SystemExit(f"check failed: {name}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_running_example() -> None:
    print("\n=== 1. A running example ===")
    D = [7, 5, 5, 3, 1, 0]
    print(f"  D = {D}")
    print(f"  tail profile  t=0..7 : {[tail(D, t) for t in range(8)]}")
    print(f"  knee profile  g=0..7 : {[knee(D, g) for g in range(8)]}")
    print(f"  sorted decreasingly  : {sorted(D, reverse=True)}")
    check("knee = order statistic at every gate",
          all(knee(D, g) == knee_order_statistic(D, g) for g in range(10)))
    check("Galois connection on a 10x10 grid",
          all((knee(D, g) <= t) == (tail(D, t) <= g) for g in range(10) for t in range(10)))
    s = sum(knee(D, g) for g in range(len(D)))
    print(f"  area identity: sum of knees g<|D| = {s},  sum(D) = {sum(D)}")
    check("area identity", s == sum(D))


def demo_random_galois_and_order_statistic(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 2000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 2. Galois connection and order statistic (random) ===")
    ok_g = ok_o = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D = random_demands(rng)
        for g in range(9):
            ok_o &= knee(D, g) == knee_order_statistic(D, g)
            for t in range(9):
                ok_g &= (knee(D, g) <= t) == (tail(D, t) <= g)
    check(f"Galois connection on {trials} random multisets", ok_g)
    check(f"order-statistic formula on {trials} random multisets", ok_o)


def demo_all_gates(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 4000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 3. All-gate theorem: knees <=> tails <=> positive demands ===")
    agree_count = 0
    ok = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D, E = random_demands(rng, 5, 3), random_demands(rng, 5, 3)
        k, t, p = all_knees_agree(D, E), all_tails_agree(D, E), positive_part(D) == positive_part(E)
        ok &= (k == t == p)
        agree_count += k
    check(f"three-way equivalence on {trials} random pairs ({agree_count} agreeing pairs)", ok)
    D, E = [4, 2, 2], [0, 2, 4, 0, 2]
    print(f"  D = {D}, D' = {E}: knees agree? {all_knees_agree(D, E)}; multisets equal? {sorted(D) == sorted(E)}")
    check("zero demands are invisible to knees", all_knees_agree(D, E) and sorted(D) != sorted(E))


def demo_window(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 6000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 4. Window theorem: gate window <=> clamped count band ===")
    D, E = [9, 6, 4, 2], [8, 6, 4, 1, 1]
    a, w = 1, 2
    print(f"  D = {D}  knees {knee_profile(D, 6)}")
    print(f"  D'= {E}  knees {knee_profile(E, 6)}")
    print(f"  window gates {list(range(a, a + w))}: agree? {knees_agree_on_window(D, E, a, w)}")
    print(f"  clamped tails of D : {[clamp_band(a, w, tail(D, t)) for t in range(10)]}")
    print(f"  clamped tails of D': {[clamp_band(a, w, tail(E, t)) for t in range(10)]}")
    check("example satisfies both sides", knees_agree_on_window(D, E, a, w) and clamped_tails_agree(D, E, a, w))
    ok = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D, E = random_demands(rng, 6, 4), random_demands(rng, 6, 4)
        a, w = rng.randint(0, 5), rng.randint(0, 4)
        lhs = knees_agree_on_window(D, E, a, w)
        ok &= lhs == clamped_tails_agree(D, E, a, w)
        if w > 0:
            ok &= lhs == band_form_agrees(D, E, a, w)
    check(f"window <=> clamp <=> band form on {trials} random instances", ok)


def demo_naive_band_false() -> None:
    print("\n=== 5. The naive closed-band formulation is false ===")
    D, E, a, b = [3], [2], 1, 1
    lhs = all(knee(D, g) == knee(E, g) for g in range(a, b + 1))
    naive = all(tail(D, t) == tail(E, t) for t in range(10) if a <= tail(D, t) <= b)
    print(f"  D={D}, D'={E}, gates [{a},{b}]: knees agree = {lhs}; naive band condition = {naive}")
    print(f"  at t = 2: tail(D,2) = {tail(D, 2)} lies in [1,1] but tail(D',2) = {tail(E, 2)}")
    check("naive formulation fails on the witness", lhs and not naive)
    w = b - a + 1
    check("the correct clamp formulation holds on the witness", clamped_tails_agree(D, E, a, w))


def demo_finite_sweep(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 3000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 6. A finite sweep of max(|D|,|D'|) gates decides everything ===")
    ok = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D, E = random_demands(rng, 5, 3), random_demands(rng, 5, 3)
        m = max(len(D), len(E))
        sweep = all(knee(D, g) == knee(E, g) for g in range(m))
        ok &= sweep == all_knees_agree(D, E)
        ok &= all(knee(D, g) == 0 for g in range(len(D), len(D) + 5))
    check(f"sweep bound on {trials} random pairs", ok)


def demo_duality(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 2000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 7. Conjugate-partition duality and the area identity ===")
    ok = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D = random_demands(rng, 8, 9)
        n, top = len(D), max(D, default=0)
        for t in range(top + 2):
            ok &= tail(D, t) == sum(1 for g in range(n) if t < knee(D, g))
        for g in range(n + 2):
            ok &= knee(D, g) == sum(1 for t in range(top) if g < tail(D, t))
        ok &= sum(knee(D, g) for g in range(n)) == sum(D)
        ok &= sum(tail(D, t) for t in range(top)) == sum(D)
    check(f"tail = conjugate of knees, knee = conjugate of tails, areas agree ({trials} trials)", ok)
    D = [5, 3, 3, 1]
    print("  Ferrers diagram of D = [5,3,3,1]: rows are knees, columns are tails")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Knee stability is equivalent to tail-exchangeability -- numerical companion.

A *demand multiset* D is a finite list of non-negative integers (order irrelevant).

  tail(D, t)  = #{ d in D : d > t }                 (upper-tail counting function)
  knee(D, g)  = least t >= 0 with tail(D, t) <= g    (knee at gate g)

This script checks, on hand-picked and random examples, every result of the paper:

  1. Galois connection      knee(D,g) <= t  <=>  tail(D,t) <= g
  2. Order statistic        knee(D,g) = g-th largest demand (0-indexed), 0 past the end
  3. All-gate theorem       knee(D,.) = knee(D',.) <=> tail(D,.) = tail(D',.)
                            <=> D and D' have the same positive demands
  4. Window theorem         knees agree for a <= g < a+w
                            <=> clamp_[a,a+w] tail(D,t) = clamp_[a,a+w] tail(D',t) for all t
  5. Naive closed band is false (explicit counterexample)
  6. Finite sweep           all-gate equality is decided by gates g < max(|D|,|D'|)
  7. Conjugate duality and the area identity  sum_{g<|D|} knee(D,g) = sum(D)
  8. Stability              (forall g: knee(D',g+k) <= knee(D,g)) <=> (forall t: tail(D',t) <= tail(D,t)+k)
                            contamination and merge bounds

Only the Python standard library is used.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import random
from collections import Counter
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Demands = Sequence[int]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core definitions
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def tail(D: Demands, t: int) -> int:
    """Number of demands strictly greater than the threshold t."""
    return sum(1 for d in D if d > t)


def knee(D: Demands, g: int) -> int:
    """Least threshold t >= 0 exceeded by at most g demands (definition by search)."""
    t = 0
    while tail(D, t) > g:
        t += 1
    return t


def knee_order_statistic(D: Demands, g: int) -> int:
    """The g-th entry (0-indexed) of D sorted in decreasing order; 0 past the end."""
    s = sorted(D, reverse=True)
    return s[g] if g < len(s) else 0


def tail_profile(D: Demands) -> List[int]:
    """tail(D, t) for t = 0 .. max(D) (it is 0 from max(D) on)."""
    top = max(D, default=0)
    return [tail(D, t) for t in range(top + 1)]


def knee_profile(D: Demands, gates: int | None = None) -> List[int]:
    """knee(D, g) for g = 0 .. gates-1 (default |D|)."""
    n = len(D) if gates is None else gates
    return [knee(D, g) for g in range(n)]


def tail_from_histogram(hist: Dict[int, int], t: int) -> int:
    """Tail computed from a histogram {value: multiplicity} -- 'one histogram per corpus'."""
    return sum(c for v, c in hist.items() if v > t)


def clamp_band(a: int, w: int, x: int) -> int:
    """Clamp the count x to the band [a, a+w]."""
    return min(max(x, a), a + w)


def positive_part(D: Demands) -> Counter:
    return Counter(d for d in D if d > 0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Predicates corresponding to the theorems
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def knees_agree_on_window(D: Demands, E: Demands, a: int, w: int) -> bool:
    return all(knee(D, g) == knee(E, g) for g in range(a, a + w))


def clamped_tails_agree(D: Demands, E: Demands, a: int, w: int) -> bool:
    top = max(max(D, default=0), max(E, default=0))
    return all(clamp_band(a, w, tail(D, t)) == clamp_band(a, w, tail(E, t))
               for t in range(top + 1))


def band_form_agrees(D: Demands, E: Demands, a: int, w: int) -> bool:
    """Below-band / above-band classification agrees and tails coincide in the open band."""
    top = max(max(D, default=0), max(E, default=0))
    for t in range(top + 1):
        x, y = tail(D, t), tail(E, t)
        if (x <= a) != (y <= a):
            return False
        if (x >= a + w) != (y >= a + w):
            return False
        if a < x < a + w and x != y:
            return False
    return True


def all_knees_agree(D: Demands, E: Demands) -> bool:
    gates = max(len(D), len(E)) + 3  # a few extra gates beyond the sweep bound
    return all(knee(D, g) == knee(E, g) for g in range(gates))


def all_tails_agree(D: Demands, E: Demands) -> bool:
    top = max(max(D, default=0), max(E, default=0)) + 2
    return all(tail(D, t) == tail(E, t) for t in range(top))


def random_demands(rng: random.Random, n_max: int = 7, v_max: int = 6) -> List[int]:
    return [rng.randint(0, v_max) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, n_max))]


def check(name: str, ok: bool) -> None:
    print(f"  [{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name}")
    if not ok:
        raise SystemExit(f"check failed: {name}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_running_example() -> None:
    print("\n=== 1. A running example ===")
    D = [7, 5, 5, 3, 1, 0]
    print(f"  D = {D}")
    print(f"  tail profile  t=0..7 : {[tail(D, t) for t in range(8)]}")
    print(f"  knee profile  g=0..7 : {[knee(D, g) for g in range(8)]}")
    print(f"  sorted decreasingly  : {sorted(D, reverse=True)}")
    check("knee = order statistic at every gate",
          all(knee(D, g) == knee_order_statistic(D, g) for g in range(10)))
    check("Galois connection on a 10x10 grid",
          all((knee(D, g) <= t) == (tail(D, t) <= g) for g in range(10) for t in range(10)))
    s = sum(knee(D, g) for g in range(len(D)))
    print(f"  area identity: sum of knees g<|D| = {s},  sum(D) = {sum(D)}")
    check("area identity", s == sum(D))


def demo_random_galois_and_order_statistic(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 2000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 2. Galois connection and order statistic (random) ===")
    ok_g = ok_o = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D = random_demands(rng)
        for g in range(9):
            ok_o &= knee(D, g) == knee_order_statistic(D, g)
            for t in range(9):
                ok_g &= (knee(D, g) <= t) == (tail(D, t) <= g)
    check(f"Galois connection on {trials} random multisets", ok_g)
    check(f"order-statistic formula on {trials} random multisets", ok_o)


def demo_all_gates(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 4000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 3. All-gate theorem: knees <=> tails <=> positive demands ===")
    agree_count = 0
    ok = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D, E = random_demands(rng, 5, 3), random_demands(rng, 5, 3)
        k, t, p = all_knees_agree(D, E), all_tails_agree(D, E), positive_part(D) == positive_part(E)
        ok &= (k == t == p)
        agree_count += k
    check(f"three-way equivalence on {trials} random pairs ({agree_count} agreeing pairs)", ok)
    D, E = [4, 2, 2], [0, 2, 4, 0, 2]
    print(f"  D = {D}, D' = {E}: knees agree? {all_knees_agree(D, E)}; multisets equal? {sorted(D) == sorted(E)}")
    check("zero demands are invisible to knees", all_knees_agree(D, E) and sorted(D) != sorted(E))


def demo_window(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 6000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 4. Window theorem: gate window <=> clamped count band ===")
    D, E = [9, 6, 4, 2], [8, 6, 4, 1, 1]
    a, w = 1, 2
    print(f"  D = {D}  knees {knee_profile(D, 6)}")
    print(f"  D'= {E}  knees {knee_profile(E, 6)}")
    print(f"  window gates {list(range(a, a + w))}: agree? {knees_agree_on_window(D, E, a, w)}")
    print(f"  clamped tails of D : {[clamp_band(a, w, tail(D, t)) for t in range(10)]}")
    print(f"  clamped tails of D': {[clamp_band(a, w, tail(E, t)) for t in range(10)]}")
    check("example satisfies both sides", knees_agree_on_window(D, E, a, w) and clamped_tails_agree(D, E, a, w))
    ok = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D, E = random_demands(rng, 6, 4), random_demands(rng, 6, 4)
        a, w = rng.randint(0, 5), rng.randint(0, 4)
        lhs = knees_agree_on_window(D, E, a, w)
        ok &= lhs == clamped_tails_agree(D, E, a, w)
        if w > 0:
            ok &= lhs == band_form_agrees(D, E, a, w)
    check(f"window <=> clamp <=> band form on {trials} random instances", ok)


def demo_naive_band_false() -> None:
    print("\n=== 5. The naive closed-band formulation is false ===")
    D, E, a, b = [3], [2], 1, 1
    lhs = all(knee(D, g) == knee(E, g) for g in range(a, b + 1))
    naive = all(tail(D, t) == tail(E, t) for t in range(10) if a <= tail(D, t) <= b)
    print(f"  D={D}, D'={E}, gates [{a},{b}]: knees agree = {lhs}; naive band condition = {naive}")
    print(f"  at t = 2: tail(D,2) = {tail(D, 2)} lies in [1,1] but tail(D',2) = {tail(E, 2)}")
    check("naive formulation fails on the witness", lhs and not naive)
    w = b - a + 1
    check("the correct clamp formulation holds on the witness", clamped_tails_agree(D, E, a, w))


def demo_finite_sweep(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 3000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 6. A finite sweep of max(|D|,|D'|) gates decides everything ===")
    ok = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D, E = random_demands(rng, 5, 3), random_demands(rng, 5, 3)
        m = max(len(D), len(E))
        sweep = all(knee(D, g) == knee(E, g) for g in range(m))
        ok &= sweep == all_knees_agree(D, E)
        ok &= all(knee(D, g) == 0 for g in range(len(D), len(D) + 5))
    check(f"sweep bound on {trials} random pairs", ok)


def demo_duality(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 2000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 7. Conjugate-partition duality and the area identity ===")
    ok = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D = random_demands(rng, 8, 9)
        n, top = len(D), max(D, default=0)
        for t in range(top + 2):
            ok &= tail(D, t) == sum(1 for g in range(n) if t < knee(D, g))
        for g in range(n + 2):
            ok &= knee(D, g) == sum(1 for t in range(top) if g < tail(D, t))
        ok &= sum(knee(D, g) for g in range(n)) == sum(D)
        ok &= sum(tail(D, t) for t in range(top)) == sum(D)
    check(f"tail = conjugate of knees, knee = conjugate of tails, areas agree ({trials} trials)", ok)
    D = [5, 3, 3, 1]
    print("  Ferrers diagram of D = [5,3,3,1]: rows are knees, columns are tails")
    for g in range(len(D)):
        print("   " + "#" * knee(D, g) + f"   knee({g}) = {knee(D, g)}")
    print("   column heights:", [tail(D, t) for t in range(max(D))])


def demo_stability(rng: random.Random, trials: int = 3000) -> None:
    print("\n=== 8. Stability: gate shifts, contamination, merging ===")
    ok_shift = ok_cont = ok_merge = True
    for _ in range(trials):
        D, E = random_demands(rng, 6, 5), random_demands(rng, 6, 5)
        k = rng.randint(0, 3)

        P = D + E

            ok_cont &= knee(D, g) <= knee(P, g) and knee(P, g + len(E)) <= knee(D, g)
            ok_merge &= max(knee(D, g), knee(E, g)) <= knee(P, g)
            for h in range(4):
                ok_merge &= knee(P, g + h) <= max(knee(D, g), knee(E, h))
    check("k-gate shift <=> uniform tail bound k", ok_shift)
    check("contamination by |E| demands moves knees by at most |E| gates", ok_cont)
    check("merge bounds max(kD(g),kE(g)) <= kDE(g) and kDE(g+h) <= max(kD(g),kE(h))", ok_merge)

    rng = random.Random(7)

algorithms.name: Construction of the Upper-Tail Step Function from a Demand Histogram
algorithms.description: A single pass counts multiplicities h(v). Sorting the V distinct values and subtracting multiplicities from the total gives tail(t) on each interval between consecutive distinct values, since tail is a right-continuous non-increasing step function that drops by h(v) at v. Time O(n + V log V), space O(V). Histograms of shards merge by addition because tail(D+E) = tail(D) + tail(E). This is the only pass over raw data the pipeline needs.
algorithms.pseudocode:
Input: demands d_1..d_n
1. h <- empty map; for i = 1..n: h[d_i] <- h[d_i] + 1
2. v_1 < ... < v_V <- sorted keys of h; running <- n
3. steps <- [(-1, n)]
4. for j = 1..V: running <- running - h[v_j]; append (v_j, running)
5. return steps   // tail(t) = running value at the largest v_j <= t (n if t < v_1)

from collections import Counter
from typing import Iterable, List, Tuple


def tail_histogram(demands: Iterable[int]) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Return the tail step function as breakpoints [(v, tail(v))] for the
    distinct values v in increasing order, plus (-1, |D|) at the front.

    tail(t) = #{d > t} is constant on [v_i, v_{i+1}) between consecutive
    distinct values, so these breakpoints determine it completely.
    """
    hist = Counter(demands)
    values = sorted(hist)
    total = sum(hist.values())
    steps: List[Tuple[int, int]] = [(-1, total)]
    running = total
    for v in values:
        running -= hist[v]          # demands equal to v no longer exceed t = v
        steps.append((v, running))
    return steps


def tail_at(steps: List[Tuple[int, int]], t: int) -> int:
    """Evaluate tail(t) from breakpoints by scanning (binary search also works)."""
    val = steps[0][1]
    for v, c in steps[1:]:
        if v <= t:
            val = c
        else:
            break
    return val


def merge_histograms(h1: Counter, h2: Counter) -> Counter:
    """Pooling: tail(D + E) = tail(D) + tail(E), so histograms simply add."""
    return h1 + h2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    D = [7, 5, 5, 3, 1, 0]
    st = tail_histogram(D)
    print(st)
    print([tail_at(st, t) for t in range(8)])   # [5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 1, 1, 0]

algorithms.name: Knee Evaluation via the Galois Connection (Order-Statistic Oracle)
algorithms.description: By the Galois connection knee(g) <= t iff tail(t) <= g, the knee is the least threshold whose tail is at most g, and equivalently the g-th largest demand. Scanning positive distinct values from the top while accumulating counts finds it in O(V); with cumulative counts and binary search, every query costs O(log V) after O(V log V) preprocessing. Zero demands never matter, which is why only positive values are stored.

Query knee(g):
1. i <- least index with c_i > g (binary search)
2. if i exists return u_i else return 0

from bisect import bisect_left
from collections import Counter
from typing import Dict, List


def knee_from_histogram(hist: Dict[int, int], g: int) -> int:
    """knee(g) = least t >= 0 with tail(t) <= g, by the Galois connection
    knee(g) <= t  <=>  tail(t) <= g.  Walk distinct values from the top,
    accumulating the tail; O(V) per query, or O(log V) with prefix sums."""
    exceed = 0
    for v in sorted(hist, reverse=True):
        # for t in [next smaller value, v), tail(t) = exceed + hist[v]
        if exceed + hist[v] > g:
            return v          # thresholds below v are exceeded by > g demands
        exceed += hist[v]
    return 0


class KneeOracle:
    """Answer many knee queries in O(log V) after O(V log V) preprocessing."""

    def __init__(self, hist: Dict[int, int]) -> None:
        self.vals: List[int] = sorted((v for v in hist if v > 0), reverse=True)
        self.cum: List[int] = []          # cum[i] = #demands >= vals[i]
        s = 0
        for v in self.vals:
            s += hist[v]
            self.cum.append(s)

    def knee(self, g: int) -> int:
        # first index i with cum[i] > g; the knee is vals[i] (order statistic)
        i = bisect_left(self.cum, g + 1)
        return self.vals[i] if i < len(self.vals) else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    D = [7, 5, 5, 3, 1, 0]
    h = Counter(D)
    oracle = KneeOracle(h)
    print([knee_from_histogram(h, g) for g in range(8)])  # [7, 5, 5, 3, 1, 0, 0, 0]
    print([oracle.knee(g) for g in range(8)])

algorithms.description: All-gate knee equality reduces to equality of positive histograms (all-gate theorem). Window equality on gates a <= g < a+w reduces to equality of clamp_[a,a+w](tail) at the merged breakpoints (window theorem), because both tails are constant between breakpoints. The gate-shift distance k* = max_t |tail_D(t) - tail_D'(t)| is the exact least mutual gate shift (gate-shift theorem). Each test costs O(V + V') once the histograms are available, for any window chosen after the fact, which replaces a G-gate sweep per cell.

# Knees, Tails, and the Histogram That Replaces a Sweep

Suppose you have a pile of jobs, each with a whole-number **demand**. You can tolerate $g$ overflows (the **gate**). What is the smallest capacity that lets all but at most $g$ jobs through? That number is the **knee** at gate $g$. This page explains why the knees of two collections agree, at all gates or on a window of gates, exactly when a single **tail histogram** says so.

## 1. Two functions, one pile

For a multiset $D$ of demands define

$$\mathrm{tail}_D(t) = \#\{d \in D : d > t\}, \qquad \mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \min\{t \ge 0 : \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le g\}.$$

For $D=\{7,5,5,3,1,0\}$ the tails at $t=0,\dots,7$ are $5,4,4,3,3,1,1,0$, and the knees at $g = 0,\dots,7$ are $7,5,5,3,1,0,0,0$. The knees are just the demands sorted from largest to smallest.

{{visualization:0}}

<details><summary>Why is the knee the $g$-th largest demand?</summary>

The threshold $d_g$ (the $g$-th largest, 0-indexed) is exceeded only by $d_0,\dots,d_{g-1}$, which is at most $g$ demands. Any smaller threshold $t<d_g$ is exceeded by all of $d_0,\dots,d_g$, which is $g+1$ demands. So $d_g$ is the least admissible threshold. Formally one shows, by induction on a non-increasing list, that $d_g \le t$ iff at most $g$ entries exceed $t$.
</details>

## 2. The switch: a Galois connection

Everything below rests on one equivalence, valid for all $g$ and $t$:

$$\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le t \iff \mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le g.$$

<details><summary>Proof (three lines)</summary>

$\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le t$ means that some $m \le t$ has $\mathrm{tail}_D(m) \le g$. Since $\mathrm{tail}_D$ is non-increasing, $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) \le \mathrm{tail}_D(m) \le g$. Conversely take $m=t$.
</details>

This is the discrete version of the relation between a survival function and a [quantile function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantile_function). It is an instance of a [Galois connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_connection).

## 3. The main theorem

> **Theorem.** For demand multisets $D, D'$ the following are equivalent:
> (1) equal knees at every gate; (2) equal tails at every threshold; (3) equal multisets of **positive** demands.

The positivity clause is needed. A zero demand never exceeds a threshold $t \ge 0$, so $\{4,2,2\}$ and $\{0,2,4,0,2\}$ have identical knees. Moreover, all-gate equality is decided by the gates $g < \max(|D|,|D'|)$, because beyond that every knee is $0$.

<details><summary>Proof sketch</summary>

(1)⇒(2): put $g=\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)$. Then $\mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g)\le t$, so $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) \le t$, so $\mathrm{tail}_D(t)\le \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)$. Swap the roles of $D$ and $D'$ for the other inequality. (2)⇒(1): at each gate the knee depends only on the up-set $\{t : \mathrm{tail}(t)\le g\}$. (2)⇔(3): the histogram is the discrete derivative of the tail, $\mathrm{tail}_D(k) = \mathrm{tail}_D(k+1) + \#_D(k+1)$.
</details>

## 4. Windows of gates and bands of counts

Usually only a window of gates $a \le g < a+w$ matters. Clamp a count to the band $[a,a+w]$ with $\mathrm{clamp}(x)=\min(\max(x,a),a+w)$.

> **Window theorem.** Knees agree for all $a \le g < a+w$ $\iff$ $\mathrm{clamp}(\mathrm{tail}_D(t)) = \mathrm{clamp}(\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t))$ for every $t$.

Equivalently, when $w>0$: at each threshold the two tails are on the same side of $a$, on the same side of $a+w$, and equal whenever strictly between. Use the explorer below. Load the **Window example**, move the sliders, and watch the two tests always agree. Then load the **Naive band trap**.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details><summary>Why the naive version fails</summary>

The naive statement says that knees agree on gates $[a,b]$ iff the tails are equal whenever $\mathrm{tail}_D(t)\in[a,b]$. Take $D=\{3\}$, $D'=\{2\}$ and the gate $1$. Both knees are $0$. But at $t=2$, $\mathrm{tail}_D = 1 \in [1,1]$ while $\mathrm{tail}_{D'} = 0$. On the band's boundary only the *side* matters, which is what the clamp captures. Note that the gate window $[a, a+w)$ corresponds to a count band $[a, a+w]$ one unit wider.
</details>

{{visualization:1}}

## 5. Conjugate partitions and the area identity

In the Ferrers diagram the rows are knees and the columns are tails. Formally, $\mathrm{tail}_D(t) = \#\{g<|D| : \mathrm{knee}_D(g) > t\}$ and $\mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \#\{t < \max D : \mathrm{tail}_D(t) > g\}$. Counting boxes gives

$$\sum_{g=0}^{|D|-1}\mathrm{knee}_D(g) = \sum_{d\in D} d.$$

See [conjugate partitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_(number_theory)#Conjugate_and_self-conjugate_partitions) for the classical background.

## 6. Stability: noise in, bounded shift out

> **Gate-shift theorem.** $\forall g:\ \mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g+k) \le \mathrm{knee}_D(g)$ $\iff$ $\forall t:\ \mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t) \le \mathrm{tail}_D(t) + k$.

So the largest gap $k^\ast=\max_t|\mathrm{tail}_D(t)-\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)|$ is exactly the smallest mutual gate shift. Consequences:

* **contamination**: $\mathrm{knee}_D(g)\le \mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g)$ and $\mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g+|E|)\le\mathrm{knee}_D(g)$;
* **merging**: $\max(\mathrm{knee}_D(g),\mathrm{knee}_E(g)) \le \mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g)$ and $\mathrm{knee}_{D+E}(g+h)\le\max(\mathrm{knee}_D(g),\mathrm{knee}_E(h))$.

Add contaminating demands below and try shifts smaller than $k^\ast$:

{{interactive_demo:1}}

{{visualization:2}}

<details><summary>Proof of the gate-shift theorem</summary>

(⇒) Set $g=\mathrm{tail}_D(t)$. Then $\mathrm{knee}_D(g)\le t$, hence $\mathrm{knee}_{D'}(g+k)\le t$, hence $\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(t)\le g+k$. (⇐) $\mathrm{tail}_{D'}(\mathrm{knee}_D(g)) \le \mathrm{tail}_D(\mathrm{knee}_D(g)) + k \le g + k$. Then apply the Galois connection.
</details>

## 7. From theory to practice: the algorithms

One pass builds the histogram. Tails of pooled collections add.

{{algorithm:0}}

Knees come out of the histogram by binary search, or as order statistics:

{{algorithm:1}}

Every comparison question (all gates, any window, the gate-shift distance) costs $O(V+V')$ on the histograms:

{{algorithm:2}}

## 8. Check everything numerically

The demo below tests every theorem on thousands of random multisets. It also shows that a 5000-item heavy-tailed corpus gives the same knees from a histogram as from a direct search.

{{demo:0}}

## Where to go next

The open directions include a full Kolmogorov-type metric built from the gate shift, real-valued weights, sampling guarantees in the style of the [DKW inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvoretzky%E2%80%93Kiefer%E2%80%93Wolfowitz_inequality), and assembling knee profiles from shard histograms. See the Future Directions tab.
